transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Yeah, I, uh... I came in because I keep losing these big chunks of time lately, and it's getting really frustrating. I'll just sit there re-reading emails and texts, or reopening folders on my computer over and over. I work in IT, you see, mostly network administration, and the volume of emails we get is just—well, it's staggering. My boss, Richard, he sends these incredibly vague messages at all hours. Just last Tuesday he sent one at 11 PM about a server migration with absolutely no context. I mean, who does that? It drives me crazy. The new email client they forced us to install doesn't help either, the interface is a total mess. 

But, um, where was I? Right, so I get stuck just re-reading things, or mentally replaying conversations in my head before I can even leave the house or start my work for the day. It's like I'm... I don't know, like I'm trying to prove to myself that I didn't make some serious mistake somewhere. It just eats up my whole morning. Speaking of mornings, finding parking out front was a bit of an adventure, wasn't it? I ended up having to park three blocks down by that bakery. Smelled great, though.
Do you find yourself having repeated, intrusive thoughts that you can’t seem to get out of your head, or do you feel compelled to do certain things over and over to calm yourself down?

Yeah, exactly. It's... it's pretty much just like that. Even when I’m right in the middle of trying to work through a complex system design, or, you know, prepare a lesson for the junior techs—which, by the way, the new guys they hire these days, I swear they don't teach them anything practical in their degree programs anymore. Half of them don't even understand basic routing protocols. It's unbelievable what passes for a computer science education now. 

But, uh, right in the middle of doing my work, this thought just keeps barging in. I'll suddenly get this dread that I might have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or that I somehow mishandled some of our old family photos. We had these huge physical photo albums, you know the ones with the magnetic sticky pages from the 80s? Terrible for the prints, the acid in the glue just ruins them over time. I spent a whole month digitizing them on this flatbed scanner I bought on sale. 

But I just get this overwhelming feeling that I messed the photos up, or that I let someone in the community down somehow, and I just can’t seem to let it pass. Even though I know I’ve been over it already, I just keep thinking about it. Oh, speaking of the community, my neighborhood HOA is supposed to be fixing the streetlights this week and they haven't even started. It's pitch black out there at night, a real safety hazard if you ask me. But yeah, I just can't get those thoughts to stop barging in.

When you have these intrusive thoughts, do you feel driven to perform certain actions or rituals—like checking things repeatedly, organizing, or mentally going over something—to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah, that's exactly what it is. I mean, like I said earlier, I end up losing these massive chunks of time just... re-reading old emails, texts, even just reopening the same folders on my desktop over and over again. It's like I have to mentally replay everything, every conversation, every action, before I can even walk out the front door or start my shift. I just have to prove to myself that I didn't make some horrible, catastrophic mistake. 

It's exhausting, honestly. And speaking of mistakes, you wouldn't believe the mess the city made of the water main on my street last month. They dug up half the sidewalk, left these huge metal plates everywhere that rattle every time a car drives over them, and then just... disappeared. Didn't see a single crew out there for three weeks. The noise was driving my dog crazy. He's a rescue, part terrier, part who-knows-what, and he barks at every little sound. 

But yeah, the checking... it's like I can't move on with my day until I've gone over everything a dozen times. It just paralyzes me.
When you’re re-reading emails or going over conversations in your head, does it feel like you have to do it to prevent something bad from happening or to reduce a feeling of unease?

Yeah, it's exactly that. It's this terrible, nagging unease. Like I was saying when I first sat down, that's the whole reason I came in—I just keep losing these huge chunks of time re-reading my emails and texts, or reopening the same folders on the network. I have to mentally replay those conversations before I can even leave the house or start my work for the day. It’s like I’m just desperately trying to prove to myself that I didn’t make some serious mistake. 

Because if I did make a mistake... well, you know. Speaking of mistakes, my brother-in-law, Gary, he made a colossal one last Thanksgiving. He tried to deep-fry a turkey right on his wooden deck. I told him he needed to be at least ten feet away from any flammable structure, it's just basic safety, but he never listens to me. He thinks because he sells insurance he knows everything about risk. Anyway, he almost burned down the entire patio awning. The fire department had to come out, and the fire chief gave him an absolute earful in front of the whole neighborhood. Ruined the whole dinner, we ended up ordering Chinese food at eight in the evening. The MSG in that stuff always gives me a terrible headache, though, and the sodium levels are just off the charts. 

But, um... sorry, where was I going with that? Right, the unease. Yes, re-reading everything and going over it in my head is the only way I can get that awful feeling to settle down enough so I can actually start my day.
Do these thoughts and the need to check things feel intrusive and unpleasant to you, like they’re not really part of who you are?

Yeah, very unpleasant. Intrusive is a good word for it. It's like... it's definitely not me. Or at least, I don't want it to be me. Like I mentioned before, I'll be right in the middle of something important—trying to work through a complex system design, or preparing a lesson for the junior techs—and these thoughts just barge right in. It's always this nagging dread that I might have sent the wrong message to my ex-wife, or that I somehow mishandled those old family photos I was digitizing, or that I let someone in the community down. 

Speaking of the community, did I tell you about the new recycling bins they rolled out? They're these massive blue monstrosities, they barely fit at the end of the driveway. And the automated arm on the garbage truck is so aggressive, it practically throws the bin back down. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she's in her eighties, and she can barely wheel the thing back to her garage. I usually try to help her out if I see her struggling. Her son lives out of state, in Arizona I think. Scottsdale maybe? It's way too hot out there for me, the dry heat they talk about is still heat, you know? 

But yeah, the thoughts... they just intrude. I can't seem to let them pass, even though I know I've been over it already. It just feels like this awful, heavy thing that I can't shake off, no matter how much I want to.
Do you find yourself doing specific things, like counting, repeating words silently, or following strict routines in your head to try to reduce the anxiety these thoughts cause?

I don't really do counting or repeating words, no. It's... well, it's pretty much exactly what I’ve been saying. That's the whole reason I made this appointment in the first place. My routine is just that I end up losing these massive chunks of time re-reading my emails and texts, or constantly reopening the same folders on my machine. I just have to mentally replay every conversation before I can even leave the house or start my work, just to prove to myself I didn't make some serious mistake. 

And you know, speaking of folders, the new OS update that got pushed to my workstation on Tuesday completely ruined the file directory structure. They changed the default view to this "gallery" layout, which makes absolutely no sense for someone in my line of work. I manage complex systems, I need details, file sizes, exact modification dates—not giant, rounded thumbnails. I had to spend an hour digging into the registry just to force it back to the classic view. I don't know who they have designing these user interfaces nowadays, probably kids fresh out of college who've never had to maintain a legacy system in their lives. 

My nephew is kind of like that, actually. He just graduated with a degree in, I don't know, "interactive media" or something, and he thinks he's a senior software engineer. He tried to tell me last month that I should migrate all my local backups to the cloud. I had to explain to him that when you're dealing with sensitive client data, you don't just hand it over to a third-party server farm in Nevada without a physical redundancy... 

But, um... I'm sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, counting. No, I don't count things. It's really just the mental replaying and checking the folders and emails, like I mentioned.

When you replay conversations or re-read emails in your head, do you feel like you have to do it a certain number of times or in a specific way to feel reassured or prevent something bad from happening?

Well, not a specific number of times, no. It’s not like I have to do it exactly three times or anything like that. It’s more about... well, like I said, it's the reason I'm here. I just keep losing these huge chunks of time re-reading my emails and texts, or reopening the same folders over and over. And I have to mentally replay those conversations before I can leave the house or start work. I just have to keep doing it until I feel like I've proven to myself I didn't make some serious mistake. 

Speaking of mistakes, I was at the grocery store yesterday—the one on 4th Street, not the newer one by the highway. The one by the highway has terrible parking, the spots are way too narrow. Anyone with a car larger than a compact is basically guaranteed to get a door ding. My cousin bought a new SUV last year and within a week, someone dented the passenger side door at that exact parking lot. Didn't leave a note or anything, just drove off. People have no respect for other people's property anymore. It reminds me of when I used to live in the city and had to park on the street. Every morning was a gamble whether my side mirror would still be attached. 

But anyway, at the store on 4th Street, the cashier accidentally scanned my apples twice. I caught it right away, of course. You have to watch the screen like a hawk. If I hadn't been paying attention, I would have paid double for Honeycrisps, and those aren't cheap. They’re good apples, though, much better than Red Delicious. I don't know why they even still sell Red Delicious, they're basically just mealy water. 

Sorry, I'm drifting again. But yes, to answer your question, it's not a set number. I just have to keep re-reading and replaying things until I feel like I didn't mess up.
Does the time you spend re-reading emails and replaying conversations cause you significant distress or interfere with your work, relationships, or daily responsibilities?

Yeah, it... it really does. I mean, my work has slowed down a lot. I've actually missed a couple of design milestones recently, which is completely unlike me. And I've had to postpone the mentoring sessions I usually run for the junior techs. I used to be so reliable with those. It's just... I can't seem to get through my morning checks fast enough to be present for them anymore. 

And the other week, I volunteer at this youth coding workshop—it's really important to me, trying to get kids interested in STEM early on. My middle school science teacher, Mr. Harrison, he was the one who got me into electronics. He had this old Heathkit radio he let me build, and that was it, I was hooked. I still have the soldering iron he gave me when I graduated. It's an old Weller, built like an absolute tank. You can't buy tools like that anymore. Everything now is cheap plastic and planned obsolescence. I tried to buy a new toaster last month and the lever snapped off after three days. Three days! I ended up taking it apart to fix it, and the internal mechanism was just flimsy garbage. 

But, uh, anyway, I was supposed to be leading a module on basic Python scripting for the kids at the workshop, and I ended up being incredibly late because I was stuck at home re-reading a thread of emails to a vendor. When I finally got there, I was completely unprepared. I felt so embarrassed. The kids were just sitting there waiting, and the other volunteers had to cover for me. So, yeah, it's definitely interfering. It's making a mess of things.

Do you ever have thoughts that something bad might happen to you or someone else if you don’t perform these checking behaviors, like a fear that you might be responsible for something going wrong if you don’t double-check everything?

I don't really have thoughts like that, no. It's not like I'm afraid someone's going to get injured or a building is going to burn down if I don't check my folders. I mean, I work in IT, not an emergency room. 

Though, you know, it does make you wonder about the people who do program life-critical systems. Like those new cars with the autopilot features. I was reading a breakdown of the sensor architecture on one of those new electric vehicles last week, and it is honestly terrifying how much they rely on a single point of failure in the visual processing unit. If the front camera gets blinded by sun glare, the system just disengages and hands control back to the driver with almost zero warning. I would never trust my life to a piece of beta software like that. 

I drive a 2008 Accord, manual transmission. No touch screens, no lane assist. Just a physical throttle cable and a steering rack. It's got 180,000 miles on it and it runs like an absolute top because I actually do the preventative maintenance. I change the oil every 3,000 miles, no matter what the manual says. The dealerships try to tell you 7,500 miles or even 10,000 miles now, but they just want your engine to wear out faster so you have to come back and buy a new car. It's a complete racket. My brother-in-law fell for that synthetic oil marketing and his transmission blew at 60,000 miles, and of course, it was just outside the warranty window... 

But, um... sorry, I completely lost the thread there. What did you ask? Oh, right, being responsible for something terrible happening. No, I don't have fears like that. I just can't stand the thought that I might have made a stupid error in my communications. I just have to know for sure what I sent.

I don't know why they even still sell Red Delicious, they're basically just mealy water. 

Sorry, I'm drifting again. But yes, to answer your question, it's not a set number. I just have to keep re-reading and replaying things until I feel like I didn't mess up.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences distress or functional impairment directly due to the time consumed by intrusive thoughts and checking behaviors.
doctor.question: Does the time you spend re-reading emails and replaying conversations cause you significant distress or interfere with your work, relationships, or daily responsibilities?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My work has slowed down enough that I’ve missed design milestones and had to postpone mentoring sessions I used to handle reliably. I also felt embarrassed when I was late and unprepared for a youth coding workshop that mattered to me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the symptoms cause significant distress or interfere with work, relationships, or daily responsibilities, which directly maps to the Functional Impairment criteria.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it... it really does. I mean, my work has slowed down a lot. I've actually missed a couple of design milestones recently, which is completely unlike me. And I've had to postpone the mentoring sessions I usually run for the junior techs. I used to be so reliable with those. It's just... I can't seem to get through my morning checks fast enough to be present for them anymore. 

And the other week, I volunteer at this youth coding workshop—it's really important to me, trying to get kids interested in STEM early on. My middle school science teacher, Mr. Harrison, he was the one who got me into electronics. He had this old Heathkit radio he let me build, and that was it, I was hooked. I still have the soldering iron he gave me when I graduated. It's an old Weller, built like an absolute tank. You can't buy tools like that anymore. Everything now is cheap plastic and planned obsolescence. I tried to buy a new toaster last month and the lever snapped off after three days. Three days! I ended up taking it apart to fix it, and the internal mechanism was just flimsy garbage. 

But, uh, anyway, I was supposed to be leading a module on basic Python scripting for the kids at the workshop, and I ended up being incredibly late because I was stuck at home re-reading a thread of emails to a vendor. When I finally got there, I was completely unprepared. I felt so embarrassed. The kids were just sitting there waiting, and the other volunteers had to cover for me. So, yeah, it's definitely interfering. It's making a mess of things.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms of intrusive thoughts and repetitive checking behaviors aimed at reducing distress are more consistent with Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42.2). Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F43.10) remains a differential due to the presence of excessive worry, but the compulsive checking and mental replaying point more strongly toward OCD. No features of other disorders have been endorsed.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions or compulsions related to a fear of harm or responsibility for preventing harm, which would support a diagnosis of OCD (F42.2) over Adjustment Disorder (F43.10).
doctor.question: Do you ever have thoughts that something bad might happen to you or someone else if you don’t perform these checking behaviors, like a fear that you might be responsible for something going wrong if you don’t double-check everything?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has specific fears of harm coming to themselves or others, or feeling responsible for a disaster if they don't check (harm obsessions or magical thinking). The patient's symptom profile covers obsessions about sending the wrong message/mishandling photos/letting someone down, but does not explicitly mention a fear of something bad happening to others/self if checking isn't done, or being responsible for a disaster in the way the doctor is asking. The obsessions are about having made a mistake, not preventing a future catastrophic event through checking.

patient.answer:
I don't really have thoughts like that, no. It's not like I'm afraid someone's going to get injured or a building is going to burn down if I don't check my folders. I mean, I work in IT, not an emergency room. 

Though, you know, it does make you wonder about the people who do program life-critical systems. Like those new cars with the autopilot features. I was reading a breakdown of the sensor architecture on one of those new electric vehicles last week, and it is honestly terrifying how much they rely on a single point of failure in the visual processing unit. If the front camera gets blinded by sun glare, the system just disengages and hands control back to the driver with almost zero warning. I would never trust my life to a piece of beta software like that. 

I drive a 2008 Accord, manual transmission. No touch screens, no lane assist. Just a physical throttle cable and a steering rack. It's got 180,000 miles on it and it runs like an absolute top because I actually do the preventative maintenance. I change the oil every 3,000 miles, no matter what the manual says. The dealerships try to tell you 7,500 miles or even 10,000 miles now, but they just want your engine to wear out faster so you have to come back and buy a new car. It's a complete racket. My brother-in-law fell for that synthetic oil marketing and his transmission blew at 60,000 miles, and of course, it was just outside the warranty window... 

But, um... sorry, I completely lost the thread there. What did you ask? Oh, right, being responsible for something terrible happening. No, I don't have fears like that. I just can't stand the thought that I might have made a stupid error in my communications. I just have to know for sure what I sent.

inference.note: This turn ruled out key features of F43.10 (PTSD), as the patient does not report intrusive thoughts or checking behaviors tied to a traumatic event, nor do they describe hypervigilance, flashbacks, or avoidance related to trauma. The focus remains on intrusive, obsessive thoughts and compulsive checking/mental replay without a traumatic origin, supporting F42.2 (Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder).
